pos: n. pl. (marginal or interlinear explanations of a text; and, in controversy, interpretations that displace what the text says)
etymology: Greek glossa, tongue, then a word needing explanation, then the explanation itself. The medieval Glossa Ordinaria was the standard commentary printed around the sacred text; Calvin's complaint is against glosses that get read instead of it.
biblical_def: A gloss is an explanation attached to a text, and it becomes a corruption when it stands in the text's place. Paul renounces the practice: “we have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience” (2Co 4:2). Peter names the danger in Paul's own letters, which the unlearned “wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction” (2Pe 3:16). The Lord's charge against the rabbinic glosses is that they nullified the text: “making the word of God of none effect through your tradition” (Mar 7:13). Jeremiah: “ye have perverted the words of the living God” (Jer 23:36). The standard is “rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines gloss as an interpretation or explanation of a word or passage; a comment; and also a specious appearance, an external show that may mislead.
webster_full: GLOSS, n. Interpretation artfully specious; a comment intended to explain or illustrate an author.
All this, without a gloss or comment, he would unriddle in a moment.
2. A specious appearance or representation; external show that may mislead an opinion.
GLOSS, v.t. To explain; to render clear and evident by comments; to illustrate.
2. To give a specious appearance to; to render specious and plausible; to palliate by specious representation.
scriptures: But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God.

As also in all his epistles, speaking in them of these things; in which are some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction.
Mar 7:13
Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition, which ye have delivered: and many such like things do ye.
And the burden of the LORD shall ye mention no more: for every man's word shall be his burden; for ye have perverted the words of the living God, of the LORD of hosts our God.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
corruption_summary: The commentary becomes the authority, and Webster's second definition names how it happens: a gloss is also a specious appearance.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster keeps both senses in one entry and the pairing is instructive. A gloss is an explanation, and a gloss is also a specious appearance that may mislead — the same word for a note in the margin and for a shine put on a thing to make it look better than it is. The overlap is not accidental. An interpretation that arrives to help a difficult verse can become the polish that keeps the reader from ever touching the verse itself, and the more useful the note, the more likely it is to be remembered in the text's place.

Second Corinthians 4:2 is the clearest description of the corruption in the New Testament and every phrase in it matters. Renounced the hidden things of dishonesty; not walking in craftiness; nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth. The Greek behind the deceitful handling is a merchant's word for adulterating goods — watering the wine. The image is not of a preacher denying the text but of one diluting it, and the test Paul supplies is that honest handling commends itself to every man's conscience, which a clever gloss never quite does.

The Reformed have no objection to notes, commentaries or study Bibles; the tradition produced a great many. The objection is to the point at which a congregation can no longer tell the difference between what the passage says and what its favourite expositor said about it. Second Peter 3:16 puts the responsibility on the reader — the unlearned and unstable wrest the Scriptures, and the ones they wrest are hard ones. The remedy in 2 Timothy 2:15 is neither to avoid the hard places nor to accept the first explanation offered, but to be a workman: study, and cut straight.
roots_summary: Greek doloo (G1389), to adulterate, handle deceitfully; strebloo (G4761), to twist, wrest; orthotomeo (G3718), to cut straight; akuroo (G208), to make of none effect.
roots_lines: Greek doloo (G1389) — to adulterate, as a merchant waters wine; 2 Corinthians 4:2 only.
Greek strebloo (G4761) — to twist, wrest; 2 Peter 3:16 only.
Greek orthotomeo (G3718) — to cut straight, rightly divide; 2 Timothy 2:15 only.
usage: “Nor handling the word of God deceitfully” — the word is a merchant's, for watering wine.
“Wrest… unto their own destruction” — and the ones wrested are the hard ones.
“Of none effect through your tradition” — the note read in the text's place.

pos: n. (foreknowledge; God's knowing of things before they come to pass)
etymology: Latin praescientia, from prae-, before, and scire, to know. The whole Arminian–Reformed dispute over election turns on what kind of knowing this is.
biblical_def: Prescience is God's foreknowledge. It is joined to His decree, not opposed to it: Christ was “delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God” (Act 2:23) — counsel and foreknowledge together, and the crucifixion was still the act of wicked hands. It governs election: “whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom 8:29); believers are “elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father” (1Pe 1:2). Its object is persons: “God hath not cast away his people which he foreknew” (Rom 11:2). And it belongs to God alone: “Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done” (Isa 46:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines prescience as foreknowledge; knowledge of events before they take place; and notes that absolute prescience belongs to God only.
webster_full: PRESCIENCE, n. Foreknowledge; knowledge of events before they take place.
Absolute prescience belongs to God only.
PRESCIENT, a. Foreknowing; having knowledge of events before they take place.
scriptures: Act 2:23
Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain:
Rom 8:29
For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren.
Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, through sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ: Grace unto you, and peace, be multiplied.
Rom 11:2
God hath not cast away his people which he foreknew. Wot ye not what the scripture saith of Elias?
Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure:
corruption_summary: Foreknowledge is made into foresight of what men will do, and Scripture's object of the verb is people rather than facts.
corruption_paragraphs: The common account has God looking down the corridor of time, seeing who will believe, and electing them on that basis — prescience as advance information. Two things stand against it. First, the grammar: Romans 8:29 and 11:2 both take a personal object. He foreknew them, not what they would do; and the Hebrew sense of knowing a person, as in You only have I known of all the families of the earth, carries love and setting apart rather than mere data. Second, the logic: if God elects on the basis of foreseen faith, the faith is the cause of the election, and Paul's whole argument in Romans 9 — not of works, but of him that calleth — collapses.

Acts 2:23 is the verse that shows the doctrine doing its proper work, and it is deliberately uncomfortable. Christ was delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, and in the same sentence Peter tells the crowd that they have taken Him and by wicked hands have crucified and slain Him. Both are asserted at full strength: the most certain event in the divine plan, and the most culpable act in human history, the same act. Every Reformed account of providence stands or falls on holding those two clauses together, and Peter states them without embarrassment or explanation.

The pastoral value of prescience is not speculative. Isaiah 46:10 is offered as a comfort to exiles — declaring the end from the beginning, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure — and it is the ground on which God distinguishes Himself from idols in that chapter. A God who merely predicts well is a spectator of the future; a God who declares the end from the beginning has one. The believer's confidence in a dark providence rests on the second, and it is worth very little if the first is all that is meant.
roots_summary: Greek prognosis (G4268), foreknowledge; proginosko (G4267), to foreknow; horizo (G3724), to mark out, determine; Hebrew yada (H3045), to know, in the sense of choosing.
roots_lines: Greek prognosis (G4268) — foreknowledge; Acts 2:23, 1 Peter 1:2 — both occurrences.
Greek proginosko (G4267) — to foreknow; Romans 8:29, 11:2, 1 Peter 1:20 — the object is always personal.
Hebrew yada (H3045) — to know, with the force of choosing; Amos 3:2, Jeremiah 1:5, Genesis 18:19.
usage: “Whom he did foreknow” — whom, not what.
“By the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God… by wicked hands” — both, in one sentence.
“Declaring the end from the beginning” — offered as comfort to exiles.

pos: n. (a calling to remembrance by an appointed act; the memorial character of the Lord's Supper)
etymology: Latin commemorare, to call to mind together, from memor, mindful. The together is not decorative: a commemoration is a corporate act, done by a people who share the memory.
biblical_def: A commemoration is an appointed act of remembrance. The Lord instituted one: “this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me” and, of the cup, “this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me” (1Co 11:24–25; Luk 22:19). It proclaims as well as recalls: “as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come” (1Co 11:26). The Passover was the pattern: “this day shall be unto you for a memorial; and ye shall keep it a feast to the LORD” (Exo 12:14). And Joshua's twelve stones were set up so that children would ask: “What mean ye by these stones?” (Jos 4:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines commemoration as the act of calling to remembrance by some solemnity; the celebration of some solemn festival for the purpose of preserving the remembrance of an event.
webster_full: COMMEMORATION, n. The act of calling to remembrance, by some solemnity; the act of honoring the memory of some person or event by solemn celebration.
The feast of shells was a commemoration of the death of their ancestors.
COMMEMORATE, v.t. To call to remembrance by a solemn act; to celebrate with honor and solemnity.
scriptures: And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me.
After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me.
For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.
And this day shall be unto you for a memorial; and ye shall keep it a feast to the LORD throughout your generations; ye shall keep it a feast by an ordinance for ever.
Jos 4:6
That this may be a sign among you, that when your children ask their fathers in time to come, saying, What mean ye by these stones?
corruption_summary: The supper is reduced to a bare memory of an absent Christ, or inflated into a fresh offering of Him.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors flank the Reformed position and each seizes a real word. Rome takes the sacrificial language and makes the Mass a re-presentation of Christ's offering, which Hebrews closes off in a single verse — by one offering He hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified — and again in the observation that a priest who offers repeatedly demonstrates the offering was insufficient. The memorialist takes in remembrance of me and concludes the supper is a mental exercise about a Christ located elsewhere. Calvin's answer is that the remembrance is real and Christ is really present to faith, feeding His people by the Spirit; the bread does not become His body, and the believer is genuinely fed.

First Corinthians 11:26 supplies the corrective to a merely inward view, because the verb is public: ye do shew the Lord's death till he come — proclaim, announce. The table preaches. A congregation eating together is making a public statement about a death, and it is doing so on a schedule that will end at a datable event, till he come. That is why the supper looks in three directions at once: back to a cross, around at a body, and forward to a return, and any account of it that keeps only the first has lost two thirds of what Paul says it does.

Joshua 4 gives the reason God appoints memorials in the first place, and it is generational. The stones were set up so that when your children ask their fathers in time to come, saying, What mean ye by these stones? there would be something to answer. Memory does not survive by itself; it survives by an act repeated in front of the young until they ask. A church that has let its ordinances become perfunctory has not merely lost a devotional benefit — it has removed the occasion of the question.
roots_summary: Greek anamnesis (G364), remembrance, a calling to mind; kataggello (G2605), to proclaim, shew forth; Hebrew zikkaron (H2146), a memorial; zakar (H2142), to remember.
roots_lines: Greek anamnesis (G364) — remembrance; Luke 22:19, 1 Corinthians 11:24–25, Hebrews 10:3.
Greek kataggello (G2605) — to proclaim, shew; 1 Corinthians 11:26, Acts 13:38, Colossians 1:28.
Hebrew zikkaron (H2146) — memorial; Exodus 12:14, 13:9, Joshua 4:7, Numbers 10:10.
usage: “This do in remembrance of me” — an appointed act, not a mood.
“Ye do shew the Lord's death till he come” — the table preaches, on a schedule.
“What mean ye by these stones?” — the memorial exists to provoke the question.

pos: v. (to seize and hold an office or authority not lawfully one's own)
etymology: Latin usurpare, to take into use, from usus, use, and rapere, to seize. The AV has it once, at 1 Timothy 2:12.
biblical_def: To usurp is to take an office not given. Paul uses the word of teaching authority in the assembly: “I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence” (1Ti 2:12). Korah's company seized the priesthood and were told, “seek ye the priesthood also?” (Num 16:10). Uzziah “went into the temple of the LORD to burn incense” and was struck with leprosy at the altar (2Ch 26:16–19). Saul forced himself and offered the burnt offering, and Samuel told him, “Thou hast done foolishly: thou hast not kept the commandment of the LORD” (1Sa 13:13). The rule is stated of the priesthood and applies wherever office is: “no man taketh this honour unto himself, but he that is called of God” (Heb 5:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines usurp as to seize and hold in possession by force or without right; as, to usurp a throne; to usurp the prerogatives of the crown.
webster_full: USURP, v.t. To seize and hold in possession by force or without right; as, to usurp a throne; to usurp the prerogatives of the crown.
USURPATION, n. The act of seizing or occupying and enjoying the property of another, without right.
2. The unlawful seizure of sovereign power.
scriptures: But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence.
And he hath brought thee near to him, and all thy brethren the sons of Levi with thee: and seek ye the priesthood also?
But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction: for he transgressed against the LORD his God, and went into the temple of the LORD to burn incense upon the altar of incense.

And Samuel said to Saul, Thou hast done foolishly: thou hast not kept the commandment of the LORD thy God, which he commanded thee: for now would the LORD have established thy kingdom upon Israel for ever.
Heb 5:4
And no man taketh this honour unto himself, but he that is called of God, as was Aaron.
corruption_summary: Usurpation is imagined as a coup, and Scripture's cases are all men who wanted to do something religious.
corruption_paragraphs: Korah, Uzziah and Saul are the three set-piece cases and none is a cynic. Korah's complaint was democratic and pious — all the congregation are holy, every one of them, wherefore then lift ye up yourselves? Uzziah was a good king, prospered by God, who went in to burn incense. Saul was facing a scattering army and a prophet who had not arrived, and he says I forced myself therefore. Each had a reasonable case, a religious motive and an urgent situation, and each was taking an office not given. That combination is what makes the doctrine hard to apply to oneself: the usurper is nearly always doing something he sincerely believes needs doing.

Hebrews 5:4 supplies the principle underneath, and it is about calling rather than competence: no man taketh this honour unto himself, but he that is called of God, as was Aaron. The verse then applies it to Christ, who glorified not himself to be made an high priest. That is the standard the passage sets — if the Son did not seize the office but received it, no one else may seize one either. Ability to do a job is not a call to it, and a church that appoints on the strength of gifting alone has adopted a different rule from the one Hebrews states.

First Timothy 2:12 is the verse most contested in the modern church and it should be handled with the care its difficulty deserves rather than with slogans. What can be said plainly is what Paul says: the prohibition is of a particular thing in a particular setting — teaching and exercising authority over men in the assembly — and the reasons he gives in the following verses are drawn from creation and the fall rather than from the customs of Ephesus. This dictionary holds the complementarian reading. It also notes that the same apostle names women as fellowlabourers in the gospel, that Priscilla helped instruct Apollos, and that any application of this text which silences women generally has gone beyond what is written.
roots_summary: Greek authenteo (G831), to exercise authority over, domineer; Hebrew maal (H4603), to trespass, act unfaithfully; lamah in the priestly sense; Greek lambano timen (G2983, G5092), to take the honour.
roots_lines: Greek authenteo (G831) — to exercise authority over; 1 Timothy 2:12 only.
Hebrew maal (H4603) — to trespass, act treacherously; 2 Chronicles 26:16, 26:18, Leviticus 5:15.
Greek ouch heauto tis lambanei ten timen (G5092) — no man taketh this honour unto himself; Hebrews 5:4–5.
usage: “Seek ye the priesthood also?” — asked of men with a democratic argument.
“I forced myself therefore” — Saul, explaining an urgent situation.
“No man taketh this honour unto himself” — and the Son did not either.

pos: n. (a vote or voice given in a choice; the congregation's part in choosing its officers)
etymology: Latin suffragium, a vote. The Reformed churches recovered the congregation's suffrage against the practice of appointment from above, on the ground that the New Testament churches had it.
biblical_def: Suffrage is the voice the people have in a choice. The New Testament churches had one. When deacons were needed, the apostles told the congregation to look out seven men, “and the saying pleased the whole multitude: and they chose Stephen” (Act 6:5). Matthias was set forth by the assembly before the lot was cast (Act 1:23–26). Elders were ordained “in every church” with the congregation present (Act 14:23). A brother was “chosen of the churches to travel with us” with the offering (2Co 8:19). And the Jerusalem decree was issued when “it pleased the apostles and elders, with the whole church” (Act 15:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines suffrage as a vote; a voice given in deciding a controverted question, or in the choice of a man for an office or trust; and united voice in competition, testimony in favor.
webster_full: SUFFRAGE, n. A vote; a voice given in deciding a controverted question, or in the choice of a man for an office or trust.
Nothing can be more grateful to a good man than to be elevated to office by the unbiased suffrages of free enlightened citizens.
2. United voice of persons in public prayer.
3. Aid; assistance. [Not in use.]
scriptures: Act 6:5

And the saying pleased the whole multitude: and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolas a proselyte of Antioch:
Act 1:23
And they appointed two, Joseph called Barsabas, who was surnamed Justus, and Matthias.
And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
And not that only, but who was also chosen of the churches to travel with us with this grace, which is administered by us to the glory of the same Lord, and declaration of your ready mind:

Then pleased it the apostles and elders, with the whole church, to send chosen men of their own company to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas; namely, Judas surnamed Barsabas, and Silas, chief men among the brethren:
corruption_summary: A congregation's voice is either abolished or absolutised, and Acts shows it exercised inside apostolic direction.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 6 is the model and its balance is easy to miss because both halves are in the same sentence. The apostles set the criteria — men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom — and the number, and they define the task. The congregation does the choosing. Then the apostles appoint the men the congregation chose. Neither party acts alone, and neither is a formality. That is what the Reformed have meant by the people's suffrage: a real voice, exercised within a real teaching authority, on candidates measured by a standard neither side invented.

Abolish the congregation's part and you get appointment from above, which is what the Reformation found and objected to — men set over churches that had never seen them, with the flock's only options being submission or departure. Absolutise it and you get a congregation that treats the pastorate as an employment decision and its own preferences as the qualification, which is the modern form of the same disease. Second Corinthians 8:19 is a useful check on both: the brother was chosen of the churches, and the purpose was that the handling of a large sum should be visibly above suspicion.

Acts 15:22 is worth noting for what it establishes about the most consequential decision the early church made. The apostles and elders deliberated; the conclusion was theirs; and it pleased them with the whole church to send chosen men to Antioch with the letter. The congregation was not polled on the doctrine of justification, and it was not bypassed either. A church order that cannot reproduce that sentence — with a real eldership and a real church, both in it — has lost something Luke thought worth recording.
roots_summary: Greek eklegomai (G1586), to choose out; cheirotoneo (G5500), to appoint, originally by show of hands; aresko (G700), to please; plethos (G4128), the multitude, the whole body.
roots_lines: Greek cheirotoneo (G5500) — to appoint; from cheir, hand — Acts 14:23, 2 Corinthians 8:19.
Greek exelexanto (G1586) — they chose; Acts 6:5, 15:22, 15:25.
Greek plethos (G4128) — the whole multitude; Acts 6:2, 6:5, 15:12, 15:30.
usage: “The saying pleased the whole multitude: and they chose” — a real voice.
“Chosen of the churches to travel with us” — and the money was the reason.
“The apostles and elders, with the whole church” — both, in one clause.

pos: adj. and n. (lying upon as a duty; and, as a noun, one who holds an office and its obligations)
etymology: Latin incumbere, to lie upon or lean on. A duty is incumbent when it rests on a man with weight — not something he may take up but something already lying there.
biblical_def: A duty is incumbent when it lies upon a man by his office or station. Paul describes his as a weight rather than a choice: “though I preach the gospel, I have nothing to glory of: for necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel” (1Co 9:16). He calls it a debt: “I am debtor both to the Greeks, and to the Barbarians; both to the wise, and to the unwise” (Rom 1:14). The watchman's duty is enforced with blood: “if thou dost not speak to warn the wicked… his blood will I require at thine hand” (Eze 33:8). Duty done earns nothing: “we are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do” (Luk 17:10). And the sum is stated: “Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man” (Ecc 12:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines incumbent as lying or resting on; and, figuratively, lying on as duty or obligation; imposed and emphatically urging or pressing to performance.
webster_full: INCUMBENT, a. Lying or resting on.
2. Lying on, as duty or obligation; imposed and emphatically urging or pressing to performance; with on or upon.
It is incumbent on every man to do good to others.
INCUMBENT, n. A person in present possession of a benefice, or of any office.
scriptures: For though I preach the gospel, I have nothing to glory of: for necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel!
Rom 1:14
I am debtor both to the Greeks, and to the Barbarians; both to the wise, and to the unwise.
Eze 33:8

When I say unto the wicked, O wicked man, thou shalt surely die; if thou dost not speak to warn the wicked from his way, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at thine hand.
So likewise ye, when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do.
Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man.
corruption_summary: Duty is discussed as though it were the enemy of grace, and the New Testament puts obligation everywhere without apology.
corruption_paragraphs: A generation of preaching anxious about legalism has left many Christians unable to hear the word duty without flinching, and the result is not more grace but less obedience and more anxiety. Scripture is untroubled. Paul says necessity is laid upon him; he calls himself a debtor; the Preacher sums the whole matter as fearing God and keeping His commandments. None of it is set against grace, and the same Paul who describes his ministry as a compulsion also says that by the grace of God he is what he is. Obligation and grace are not competitors in the New Testament; the obligation follows from what grace has already done.

Luke 17:10 is the verse that keeps duty from becoming merit, and it is one of the hardest sentences the Lord speaks: when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants; we have done that which was our duty to do. Not if ye have done all — when. Even complete obedience creates no credit, because a servant doing his work has not conferred a favour on his master. That kills merit at the root, and it also settles the resentment that grows in a man who thinks his faithfulness has earned him a claim on God.

Ezekiel 33 gives the heaviest form the doctrine takes and it applies to any man in office. The watchman who warns has delivered his soul whatever the city does; the watchman who does not warn is charged with the blood. He is not made responsible for the outcome — the wicked man dies in his iniquity either way — but he is entirely responsible for the warning. That is a mercy as well as a terror, since it fixes the boundary of what a minister, an elder, or a father must answer for, and the boundary is his own faithfulness rather than another man's response.
roots_summary: Greek anagke (G318), necessity; opheiletes (G3781), a debtor; achreios (G888), unprofitable; Hebrew darash (H1875), to require, seek.
roots_lines: Greek anagke epikeitai (G318, G1945) — necessity is laid upon; 1 Corinthians 9:16.
Greek opheiletes (G3781) — debtor; Romans 1:14, 8:12, 15:27, Galatians 5:3.
Hebrew damo miyadeka abaqqesh (H1245) — his blood will I require at thine hand; Ezekiel 3:18, 33:8.
usage: “Necessity is laid upon me” — a weight, not a choice.
“When ye shall have done all… we are unprofitable servants” — when, not if.
“His blood will I require at thine hand” — the warning, not the outcome.

pos: adj. (pertaining to the clergy; belonging to the ordained ministry as a distinct order)
etymology: Greek kleros, a lot or inheritance — and here is the irony that governs the whole entry: 1 Peter 5:3 uses kleros of the flock, warning elders not to be lords over God's heritage. The word that became “clergy” is the Bible's word for the laity.
biblical_def: Clerical describes the ordained as a class. The New Testament's word-history runs the other way: elders are told to feed the flock, “neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock” (1Pe 5:3) — and heritage there is kleros, the root of clergy, used of the congregation. Office exists to equip, not to replace: Christ gave pastors and teachers “for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ” (Eph 4:11–12). Gifts are distributed to all: “the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal” (1Co 12:7). The whole church is a priesthood (1Pe 2:9). And the apostles kept to their own work: “we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word” (Act 6:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines clerical as relating to the clergy, or to a clerk; and clergy as the body of men set apart, by due ordination, to the service of God in the Christian church.
webster_full: CLERICAL, a. Relating or pertaining to the clergy; as clerical tonsure; clerical robes; clerical duties.
CLERGY, n. The body of men set apart, by due ordination, to the service of God, in the christian church.
The word is derived from the Greek word signifying a lot, inheritance or portion.
scriptures: Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.
Eph 4:11
And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers;
Eph 4:12
For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ:
But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal.
Act 6:4
But we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word.
corruption_summary: The ministry becomes a caste, and Ephesians 4 gives it as an equipping office for a working church.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster's own entry preserves the point without pressing it: the word comes from the Greek for a lot or inheritance. In 1 Peter 5:3 that word names the flock — God's heritage, His allotted portion — and the elders are warned not to lord it over them. Somewhere between the apostle and the Middle Ages the term migrated from the people to the officers, and the migration was not a mere accident of vocabulary; it marked a church in which the ordained had become the church and the rest had become its audience.

Ephesians 4:11–12 gives the corrective and its punctuation matters. Christ gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body. Read straight, the officers equip the saints, and the saints do the work of the ministry. That single clause reorganises a congregation: the pastor is not the man who does the church's work while others watch, but the man whose work is to make the others able. The chapter's endpoint is a body in which every joint supplieth and every part works in measure.

None of this abolishes the office, and the anticlerical reading of these verses is its own error. Acts 6 exists precisely because the apostles refused to be diverted from prayer and the ministry of the word — they created an office rather than diluting theirs. First Timothy says elders who rule well are worthy of double honour, and Hebrews tells a congregation to obey them that have the rule over them. The Reformed position is neither a priestly caste nor a church with no officers, but ordained men who are inside the brotherhood and accountable within it, doing a distinct work for a congregation that has work of its own.
roots_summary: Greek kleros (G2819), a lot, inheritance, heritage; katartismos (G2677), perfecting, equipping; diakonia (G1248), ministry, service; phanerosis (G5321), manifestation.
roots_lines: Greek kleros (G2819) — lot, heritage; 1 Peter 5:3 — of the flock; also Acts 1:26, Colossians 1:12.
Greek katartismos (G2677) — perfecting, equipping; Ephesians 4:12 only.
Greek diakonia (G1248) — ministry, service; Ephesians 4:12, Acts 6:4, 2 Corinthians 5:18.
usage: “Lords over God's heritage” — and heritage is the word that became clergy.
“For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry” — read straight.
“Given to every man to profit withal” — every man.

pos: adj. (deserving to be cursed; accursed; detestable)
etymology: Latin execrabilis, from ex- and sacer, sacred — to execrate is to devote out of the sacred, to place under a curse. The AV's word is accursed, and the Greek is anathema.
biblical_def: An execrable thing is one placed under a curse. Paul pronounces it on a doctrine, twice, including against himself: “though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8), and on a settled disposition: “If any man love not the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema” (1Co 16:22). Achan's theft made a whole camp accursed: “neither will I be with you any more, except ye destroy the accursed from among you” (Jos 7:12). The Law placed the hanged man under it: “he that is hanged is accursed of God” (Deu 21:23). And that is where the doctrine turns: “Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us” (Gal 3:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines execrable as deserving to be cursed; very hateful; detestable; abominable; and execrate as to curse, to denounce evil against.
webster_full: EXECRABLE, a. Deserving to be cursed; very hateful; detestable; abominable.
EXECRATE, v.t. To curse; to denounce evil against, or to imprecate evil on; to abominate; to abhor.
EXECRATION, n. The act of cursing; a curse pronounced; imprecation of evil.
scriptures: Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
If any man love not the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema Maranatha.
Jos 7:12

Therefore the children of Israel could not stand before their enemies, but turned their backs before their enemies, because they were accursed: neither will I be with you any more, except ye destroy the accursed from among you.

His body shall not remain all night upon the tree, but thou shalt in any wise bury him that day; (for he that is hanged is accursed of God;) that thy land be not defiled, which the LORD thy God giveth thee for an inheritance.
Gal 3:13
Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree:
corruption_summary: The anathema is used as a weapon in disputes it was never meant for, and the one place it lands hardest is on Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Galatians 1:8 is the strongest sentence in the New Testament and the church has repeatedly borrowed its force for arguments Paul never had in mind. What is under the curse there is another gospel — specifically, the addition of circumcision to faith as a condition of acceptance with God. Not a difference over church order, or eschatology, or a translation, or a hundred things over which anathemas have since been pronounced. The verse's own guard is the clause including the apostle and an angel: a man who invokes it must be prepared to stand under the same standard, and the willingness to do that is rare among people who quote it.

Joshua 7 shows how seriously the Old Testament takes the category and why. The accursed thing in Achan's tent was not merely his private sin; it made the entire camp accursed, so that Israel could not stand before its enemies until it was dealt with. That is the doctrine of corporate holiness in its hardest form, and it lies behind the New Testament's instruction to put away from among yourselves that wicked person. A church that cannot bring itself to deal with a known and unrepented evil has not been merciful; it has left the thing in the camp.

Then Galatians 3:13 turns the whole doctrine round, and it does so by quoting Deuteronomy 21:23. Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree. The execrable thing on the hill outside the city was the Son of God, placed under the curse by law and by design, so that those who were under it might be bought out. Every anathema in the Bible is answered there, and no Christian may pronounce one without remembering who took the last one.
roots_summary: Greek anathema (G331), a thing devoted to destruction, accursed; katara (G2671), a curse; Hebrew cherem (H2764), a devoted thing; qelalah (H7045), a curse.
roots_lines: Greek anathema (G331) — accursed, devoted to destruction; Galatians 1:8–9, 1 Corinthians 16:22, Romans 9:3.
Hebrew cherem (H2764) — a devoted or accursed thing; Joshua 6:17–18, 7:1, 7:11–13.
Greek katara (G2671) — curse; Galatians 3:10, 3:13, Hebrews 6:8, James 3:10.
usage: “Though we, or an angel from heaven” — and he includes himself.
“Except ye destroy the accursed from among you” — it was in the camp.
“Being made a curse for us” — where every anathema is answered.

pos: n. pl. (evasions; shifts resorted to in order to escape a charge or an obligation)
etymology: Latin subterfugere, to flee by stealth, from subter, beneath, and fugere, to flee — an escape made underneath rather than in the open.
biblical_def: A subterfuge is an evasion offered in place of a confession, and the Bible's first recorded conversation after the Fall is made of them. Adam: “The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat” (Gen 3:12). Eve: “The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat” (Gen 3:13). Saul, confronted with the bleating of the sheep: “the people spared the best of the sheep and of the oxen, to sacrifice unto the LORD thy God” (1Sa 15:15). Judah under Jeremiah: “Yet thou sayest, Because I am innocent, surely his anger shall turn from me” (Jer 2:35). And the verdict: “He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy” (Pro 28:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines subterfuge as that to which a person resorts for escape or concealment; a shift; an evasion; an artifice employed to escape censure or the force of an argument.
webster_full: SUBTERFUGE, n. Literally, that to which a person resorts for escape or concealment; hence, a shift; an evasion; an artifice employed to escape censure or the force of an argument, or to justify opinions or conduct.
scriptures: Gen 3:12
And the man said, The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat.
Gen 3:13
And the LORD God said unto the woman, What is this that thou hast done? And the woman said, The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat.
And Saul said, They have brought them from the Amalekites: for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the oxen, to sacrifice unto the LORD thy God; and the rest we have utterly destroyed.
Jer 2:35
Yet thou sayest, Because I am innocent, surely his anger shall turn from me. Behold, I will plead with thee, because thou sayest, I have not sinned.
He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.
corruption_summary: Every subterfuge in Scripture contains a true statement, which is exactly what makes it a subterfuge.
corruption_paragraphs: The striking feature of Genesis 3:12 is that Adam is not lying. The woman did give him the fruit, and God did give him the woman. Every clause is accurate, and the whole is an evasion — because the question was hast thou eaten? and the answer is a history of how it came about, ending, almost as an afterthought, with and I did eat. That is the anatomy of the thing. A subterfuge rarely needs a falsehood; it needs a set of true facts arranged so that the speaker is the last item and the smallest.

Saul's version adds a religious motive, which is the most durable form of the shift. The people spared the best of the sheep to sacrifice unto the LORD thy God — note the pronoun, and note that Samuel had just heard the animals. Every element is deployed to distribute the responsibility: the people did it, the intention was worship, and the God in question is Samuel's. The prophet's reply cuts through all three at once: hath the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice.

Proverbs 28:13 states the alternative in the fewest possible words, and its promise is the reason the whole subject matters. He that covereth his sins shall not prosper — the covering is exhausting, and it never finishes, since each concealment requires the next. But whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy. Two verbs, and neither works alone: confession without forsaking is sentiment, forsaking without confession is reform. What waits at the end of both is mercy, which no subterfuge has ever obtained for anyone.
roots_summary: Hebrew kasah (H3680), to cover, conceal; yadah (H3034), to confess; chamal (H2550), to spare; Greek prophasis (G4392), a pretext.
roots_lines: Hebrew kasah (H3680) — to cover, conceal; Proverbs 28:13, Psalm 32:5, Job 31:33.
Hebrew yadah (H3034) — to confess, acknowledge; Proverbs 28:13, Leviticus 5:5, Psalm 32:5.
Greek prophasis (G4392) — pretext, pretence; Matthew 23:14, John 15:22, Philippians 1:18.
usage: “The woman whom thou gavest to be with me” — every clause true.
“To sacrifice unto the LORD thy God” — and Samuel could hear the sheep.
“Whoso confesseth and forsaketh” — two verbs, and neither works alone.

pos: v. (to rail against; to attack with harsh and abusive words)
etymology: Latin invehi, to be carried against, from in- and vehere, to carry. To inveigh is to be carried at someone — the momentum is in the word.
biblical_def: To inveigh is to rail. Scripture restrains it at a surprising level: “Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee” (Jud 1:9); and “angels, which are greater in power and might, bring not railing accusation against them before the Lord” (2Pe 2:11). The rule for Christians is general: “speak evil of no man, to be no brawlers, but gentle, shewing all meekness unto all men” (Tit 3:2); “not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing” (1Pe 3:9). Paul withdraws a word instantly on learning it was addressed to the high priest: “Thou shalt not speak evil of the ruler of thy people” (Act 23:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines inveigh as to exclaim or rail against; to utter censorious and bitter language against any one; to reproach; and inveigher as a railer, a vehement declaimer.
webster_full: INVEIGH, v.i. To exclaim or rail against; to utter censorious and bitter language against any one; to reproach; to abuse; with against.
Men inveigh against the follies and vices of the age.
INVEIGHER, n. One who inveighs; a railer; a vehement declaimer.
scriptures: Jud 1:9
Yet Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee.
Whereas angels, which are greater in power and might, bring not railing accusation against them before the Lord.
Tit 3:2
To speak evil of no man, to be no brawlers, but gentle, shewing all meekness unto all men.
Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing; knowing that ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing.
Act 23:5
Then said Paul, I wist not, brethren, that he was the high priest: for it is written, Thou shalt not speak evil of the ruler of thy people.
corruption_summary: Vehemence is taken for conviction, and Jude's example of restraint is an archangel addressing the devil.
corruption_paragraphs: Jude 1:9 is the argument from the extreme case, and it is chosen deliberately. If any speaker ever had standing to rail, it is an archangel; if any target ever deserved it, it is the devil. Michael durst not bring a railing accusation, and said instead, The Lord rebuke thee — four words that refer the matter to a higher authority rather than settling it with abuse. Jude's point is not that the devil deserves courtesy but that railing is a presumption on the part of the railer, taking a judgment that belongs to God.

The confusion in the church is between vehemence and conviction, and they are not the same faculty. Scripture contains a great deal of severe speech: the Lord's woes on the Pharisees, Paul's wish about the circumcision party, the prophets on the shepherds of Israel. What distinguishes those from railing is that each is a specific charge, laid by someone with standing, with a purpose beyond the wounding, and delivered by men who could also weep over the same people. Titus 3:2 supplies the ordinary rule for everyone else — speak evil of no man, be no brawlers, gentle, shewing all meekness unto all men — and the following verse gives the reason: for we ourselves also were sometimes foolish.

Acts 23:5 is the practical model and its speed is the point. Paul, struck on the mouth by order of the man presiding, says something sharp, and on being told he has spoken to the high priest, withdraws it at once and quotes the commandment against himself. He does not defend it on the ground that the man was in fact a whited wall, which he was, or that the blow was unjust, which it was. The reflex to check whether one's words are lawful, rather than whether they are deserved, is what the passage is showing, and it is the discipline most missing from religious argument in any century.
roots_summary: Greek blasphemia / blasphemos (G988, G989), railing, evil speaking; loidoria (G3059), reviling; amachos (G269), not a brawler; krisis blasphemias (G2920), a railing accusation.
roots_lines: Greek krisin blasphemias (G2920, G988) — a railing accusation; Jude 1:9, 2 Peter 2:11.
Greek loidoria (G3059) — reviling, railing; 1 Peter 3:9, 1 Timothy 5:14.
Greek amachos (G269) — not a brawler, not contentious; Titus 3:2, 1 Timothy 3:3.
usage: “Durst not bring against him a railing accusation” — an archangel, to the devil.
“The Lord rebuke thee” — four words, referring it upward.
“I wist not, brethren, that he was the high priest” — withdrawn at once.
